document_brief.narrative_theme: This study quantifies how distribution centre configuration, carrier lane performance, and last-mile cost drivers interact to raise cost-to-serve, then recommends network changes that reduce total logistics cost while protecting service levels.

sections.heading: Distribution Centre Configuration Scenarios and Total Cost-to-Serve Impact
key_facts: Baseline FY2025 network operates 3 distribution centres: Dallas, TX; Columbus, OH; and Reno, NV.
Scenario S2 consolidates to 2 distribution centres (Dallas, TX and Columbus, OH) and increases total cost-to-serve by 4.8% versus baseline.
Scenario S4 adds a new distribution centre in Atlanta, GA (go-live 2026-01-01) and reduces total cost-to-serve by 6.2% versus baseline.

structure.heading: Distribution Centre Configuration Scenarios and Total Cost-to-Serve Impact
text_content: **Distribution Centre Configuration Scenarios and Total Cost-to-Serve Impact**

The baseline FY2025 network operates three distribution centres: Dallas, TX; Columbus, OH; and Reno, NV. This configuration serves current demand footprints with established inventory pools and carrier lanes, and provides geographic coverage across the South, Midwest, and West. Baseline assumptions used for comparisons include existing service commitments, routing patterns, and steady-state inventory turns under FY2025 demand. Performance reporting and cost attribution in this study use the Baseline to normalize transport, handling, and fulfilment costs so percentage impacts of alternate scenarios are comparable on a like-for-like basis.

Scenario S2 consolidates to 2 distribution centres (Dallas, TX and Columbus, OH) and increases total cost-to-serve by 4.8% versus baseline. While fixed facility overhead declines, outbound miles to customers previously served from Reno, NV increase, which raises parcel and LTL spend and drive-time costs. Centralising inventory requires higher safety stock in Dallas and Columbus to maintain service levels, increasing carrying costs. Operational risks include dock capacity pressure and peak-period service degradation; mitigation options include adjusted routing, temporary cross-dock capacity, and focused carrier rate negotiations.

The Atlanta node improves proximity to Southeast demand, lowering last-mile miles, regional LTL rates, and expedited parcel premiums; these transport savings outweigh site setup and incremental operating costs. Implementation should follow a phased plan with go-live readiness testing, carrier onboarding, and inventory seeding. Post-implementation KPIs to track include total cost-to-serve, transit time by zone, fill rate, and DC throughput against the 2026 operational plan.

text_content: **Carrier Lane Performance, Last-Mile Cost Drivers, and Recommended Network Changes**

In 2025 Q2 the Los Angeles, CA → Phoenix, AZ linehaul lane averaged $2.18 per mile with 86% on‑time performance, indicating a mix of competitive pricing and service inconsistency. This performance point should be treated as a benchmark for comparable West‑coast corridors; lanes under $2.50 per mile with ≥90% on‑time should be prioritized for volume consolidation, while lanes performing below 85% require operational review, carrier accountability clauses, and potential retendering to protect customers.

Last‑mile cost analysis identifies density, stop type, and failed delivery rates as primary drivers. Notably, residential delivery stops average $6.40 more per stop than commercial stops in FY2025, a delta that disproportionately increases costs in suburban and low‑density routes. Mitigation levers include route density improvement, appointment‑window optimization, and consumer surcharge policies. Carrier selection should weight last‑mile cost per stop and failed‑delivery frequency alongside transit time to deliver realistic cost‑to‑serve assessments and margin impact.

Recommended change set R1 (activate Atlanta, GA DC + rebid top 20 lanes) targets $12.4M annualised savings with a 9‑month payback. Immediate actions include DC activation project plan, carrier rebid timelines, negotiation templates, and KPI baselines for cost, service, and capacity. Anticipated risks are transition volume volatility, implementation costs, and temporary service degradation; mitigation requires phased cutovers, dedicated carrier change management, and weekly executive reviews during the nine‑month payback window and measurable milestones.
